method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
Magnification links three quantities: \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}\). You are given two and find the third.

The rule that saves most marks: both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide, so convert first. Going to a smaller unit (mm → μm → nm) multiply by 1000; going larger, divide by 1000.

Rearrange when needed: actual size = image ÷ magnification, image size = magnification × actual. Magnification has no unit.

steps: Multi-step questions chain a conversion with a calculation, or compare two cells.
To compare sizes fairly, work out each actual size first, then subtract or divide. Never compare image sizes directly.
For very small lengths, finish in standard form: one digit before the point, then the power of 10.

misconceptions.message: Magnification = 45 ÷ 0.015 = 3000. Actual size = 0.015 mm = 15 μm, which fits an animal cell (10–30 μm).
0.015 mm = 15 μm (×1000). 15 μm is too big for a bacterium (1–5 μm); it fits an animal cell.

guided_steps.say: Magnification = image ÷ actual with both in the same unit. The actual size is in nm, so convert the image all the way to nm.

misconceptions.message: The actual size is in nm, so convert the image to nm too: 18 mm = 18,000,000 nm. Converting only to μm (18,000) and dividing by 300 wrongly gives 60.

gold.hint: Work out each actual size, then compare those, not the image sizes.
gold.display: A student measures the image of a bacterial cell as 14 mm under ×4000 magnification. Another student measures the image of a plant cell as 48 mm under ×800 magnification. Which cell has the larger actual size, and by how many μm?

misconceptions.message: Bacterium: 14 mm = 14,000 μm, actual = 14,000 ÷ 4000 = 3.5 μm. Plant: 48 mm = 48,000 μm, actual = 48,000 ÷ 800 = 60 μm. Difference = 60 − 3.5 = 56.5 μm.
Compare actual sizes, not image sizes. A larger image at a higher magnification can still be a smaller cell.
